analysis.one_liner: Delays Medicare price negotiation for gene-targeted drugs by four extra years.
analysis.headline: The bill to delay Medicare negotiation for genetically targeted drugs has 50 bipartisan cosponsors but has not advanced past its first committee referral since February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program lets Medicare negotiate lower prices for the most expensive drugs once they have been on the market for a set period — 7 years for ordinary drugs, 11 years for biologics. This bill says that drugs built on genetically targeted technology (like RNA-based therapies) must wait 11 years instead of 7 before Medicare can negotiate their price. That gives makers of these high-priced drugs roughly four more years of sales before the government can push the price down. The bill was referred to two House committees in February 2025 and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of genetically targeted drug products — RNA-based and other gene-modulating therapies, which are typically among the most expensive drugs on the market. They would keep charging pre-negotiation prices for up to four additional years before Medicare can select their drugs for price negotiation.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, a drug product qualifies for Medicare price negotiation once it has had market approval for at least 7 years; the bill would require genetically targeted drug products to have 11 years of market approval first.
The bill defines 'advanced drug product' as a drug that incorporates or uses a genetically targeted technology that modulates the function of a gene or its gene product.
The delay applies to the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program created to negotiate prices of certain high-cost prescription drugs under Medicare beginning in 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare, and the taxpayers and beneficiaries who fund it, would pay higher prices for gene-targeted drugs for up to four more years than under current law. Medicare program savings from negotiating those drugs' prices would be postponed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare and its taxpayers and beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Delaying negotiation eligibility for these drugs postpones Medicare savings and keeps out-of-pocket costs higher for beneficiaries for up to four additional years.

Genetically targeted therapies are among the most expensive drug classes; extending the pre-negotiation window for that class concentrates the delay on the drugs where price negotiation would matter most.

Supporters' best-faith argument — that gene-targeted technologies need more years to recoup research investment — is a claim about industry incentives, not a guarantee that savings will reach patients; the bill contains no provision requiring any offsetting benefit for beneficiaries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes almost entirely to the makers of gene-targeted drugs, in the form of up to four extra years of un-negotiated Medicare pricing. The cost falls on Medicare spending and, indirectly, on beneficiaries and taxpayers. Supporters argue the longer runway protects investment in new gene-based therapies for serious diseases, but the bill includes no mechanism ensuring any of that revenue reaches patients in the form of lower prices or better access, and it does nothing for the ordinary family except delay possible price relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 27, 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald G. Davis (D-NC) introduced the bill on February 27, 2025, with 13 original cosponsors from both parties.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee; no further action has been recorded since the referral.
The bill has attracted 50 cosponsors, including 43 of the 223 House Republicans and 7 of the 217 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, makers of genetically targeted drugs: Medicare price negotiation for their products remains on the current timeline, and the bill that would delay it has not moved — but neither has any competing measure tightening negotiation, so the status quo on their pricing stands. The main beneficiary of the bill's stall is anyone counting on negotiation savings, while the industry keeps the option open if it later gains traction.

sides.party_line_note: Support is bipartisan but lopsided: 43 of 223 House Republicans and 7 of 217 House Democrats have signed on, and no senator or committee has opposed the bill on the record because it has not received any action beyond referral.

industries.industry: Brand-name makers of genetically targeted drugs
industries.note: The bill gives gene-targeted drug products up to four extra years before Medicare can negotiate their prices, extending the period they can charge un-negotiated prices on a program whose negotiation savings would otherwise come at their expense. Because these therapies are among the most expensive on the market, the delay is worth the most precisely where negotiation would cut the deepest.

Not an industry, but the paying side: postponing negotiation eligibility postpones Medicare's negotiated savings on these drugs, which is cost borne by the program's budget and by beneficiaries through premiums and cost-sharing.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in two committees with no scheduled hearing or markup. Bipartisanships of this size (50 cosponsors) rarely guarantees floor time; similar Medicare-negotiation-delay measures have historically needed to ride on a larger package to move. Unless it is attached to broader health or drug legislation, its likely path is to die quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress.
